terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives termes as a later spelling of tarmes, the woodworm (Isidore, Servius); the zoologists took it as the name of the termites, and so it is used here, a modern sense of an old word. The same spelling is also a different classical word, a lopped bough of olive (Hor. Epod. 16.45).

terms.gloss: a woodworm, a grub that eats timber
evidence: Plaut. Most. 825: ambō ab īnfimō tarmes secat

phrases.latin: Termitēs tignum exēdērunt; nunc cavum est.
phrases.english: The termites have eaten away the beam; now it’s hollow.

phrases.latin: Vidē hunc tumulum: termitēs eum aedificāvērunt.
phrases.english: Look at this mound: termites built it.

phrases.latin: Quia edepol ambō ab īnfimō tarmes secat.
phrases.english: Because, heavens, the woodworm is eating them both away from the bottom.
